transcript:
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder. Ukraine's president is urging world leaders
to help end what he calls Russia's crazy war against his country. The US and European countries
are worried that the conflict is spreading. NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports from the
UN General Assembly in New York.
>> Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky says it's madness that Russia keeps fighting to
try to take Ukrainian land, even as Ukrainian drones and missiles damage Russia's energy
sector. He's offered a ceasefire if Russia stops bombing civilian infrastructure and
blocking grain shipments. Secretary of State Marco Rubio came out of talks with Russia's
foreign minister, saying both sides are interested in limited steps on grain and energy.
>> It doesn't solve the war, but it does, I think, in some ways potentially alleviate
some of the global pressures that are being felt as a result of that.
>> But Europeans say Russia is expanding the conflict and threatening NATO airspace. The
US ambassador, Mike Waltz, calls that unacceptable. Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, New York.
>> A federal judge in Washington, DC heard arguments Wednesday on President Trump's decision
to ban CNN, MS Now, and Politico from the White House grounds. The case is billed as a major
test of the First Amendment, but NPR's David Focomflic says it could hinge on due process
as well.
>> The judge, Timothy Kelly, right off the bat said, look, I think there are real problems.
There's strong indications that the federal government, the administration violated the
Fifth Amendment rights of these media outlets, and that's the due process clause. That is,
the president sort of announced he wanted to do these things on social media on Friday.
He said so again to reporters later that afternoon, and then over the weekend, the White House
scrambled to make it so. That's not a process by which the reporters and their outlets learn
what they may have done to offend, and do they have a process to appeal this?
>> The judge did not rule from the bench, but he said he will decide the case as soon
as possible. Experts in policing and privacy testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee
at a Wednesday hearing on flock surveillance cameras. Those AI-powered license plate readers
facing intense bipartisan backlash after reports of police officers abusing or misusing the
technology, as NPR's Meg Anderson reports.
>> Senators from both parties want more guardrails for the technology, which captures billions
of license plates every month and can track people over time. Missouri Senator Josh Hawley,
a Republican, said flock is treating all Americans like criminals. One witness at the hearing,
Lindsay Isaacs, has personal experience with that. She was wrongly accused of causing a
fatal car accident. She spent two weeks in jail, including in solitary confinement.
>> I was terrified. I was facing the possibility of spending the rest of my life in prison
for a crash that I knew I had not been involved in.
>> Senator Hawley said he invited the CEO of flock and several other surveillance companies
to testify, but they did not attend.
>> You're listening to NPR News. The FBI's jobs portal remains inaccessible amid an investigation
into a hacking group's claims that it breached the bureau's computer system and stole data
on thousands of current and former FBI employees and job applicants. The group's claims have
not been verified. The FBI says it is aware of the claims, but that the point of breach
has yet to be determined. Fighting erupted Wednesday in the Tigray region of northern
Ethiopia, where local leaders have announced what they call a defensive war against the
central government. Emmet Livingstone reports.
>> Hundreds of thousands of people were killed in the civil war that ravaged Ethiopia between
2020 and 2022. That conflict pitted the Ethiopian government against rebels from the northern
Tigray region. Now, after months of escalating tensions, the country is tipping back into
open war. The Tigrayan People's Liberation Front announced that it was again entering
hostilities, which it called defensive against the government. According to the news agency
AFP, the rebels have already captured airports in Tigray and have clashed with government
troops. The sudden escalation comes after the Tigrayan rebels, as well as six other armed
groups in Ethiopia, announced an alliance on Sunday and vowed to overthrow the government
of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. The conflict looks set to expand. For NPR News, I'm Emmet
Livingstone.
>> Stocks in Asia are mostly declining. However, Japan's benchmark Nikkei is gaining ground
up 1.3% by the midday break. Japanese stocks are advancing after Wall Street posted losses
amid pressure from the U.S. bond market. I'm Giles Snyder, NPR News.
